profile.reading:
Crane DC - Portland is a data center campus under construction in Forest Grove, Oregon, roughly eight miles from Hillsboro and about 25 miles west of downtown Portland, developed by Crane Data Centers Inc., a San Francisco-based data center developer, in partnership with Principal Real Estate Investors. The site occupies about 35 acres on Heather Street, a parcel bordered by existing residential neighborhoods on two sides, in an area zoned light industrial since 1980, a designation that predates data centers as a land use in Washington County and has not been rewritten to address them specifically.

The project's path to approval was not quiet. Plans were first announced in early 2023, and Forest Grove's Planning Division approved the project on July 31, 2024. A neighboring property owner appealed, and the Planning Commission reaffirmed the approval on a 4 to 2 vote that September, after which some residents reportedly walked out of the meeting in protest. Crane broke ground on the first phase in July 2025. As a condition of approval, Crane is required to fund an extension of Heather Street between Mountain View Lane and Poplar Street and to pay for the electrical infrastructure upgrades the campus requires.

Local and trade-press coverage of the permitted project describes two buildings roughly 179,000 square feet apiece, one about 40 to 45 feet tall and a second, later phase around 70 to 75 feet tall, with the campus's initial power draw starting near 8 to 50 megawatts and headroom to expand beyond 100 megawatts at full build-out. Site work includes off-street parking, two stormwater quality facilities, an equipment yard, and landscaping. Crane's own marketing materials describe the same campus using different phase names, PDX01 and PDX02, citing 36,000 square feet of white space plus 6,400 square feet of support space per PDX01 phase at 24 megawatts each, and roughly 150,000 square feet and 48 megawatts for PDX02, for a stated campus total exceeding 100 megawatts, with PDX02 targeted ready for service in the third quarter of 2026. The gap between the white-space figures in Crane's marketing copy and the larger total building footprints described in local permit coverage most likely reflects the difference between raised-floor technical space and each building's full footprint, including support, mechanical, and electrical plant, a distinction Crane has not published a figure reconciling.

During the approval process, neighbors raised concerns over noise, light pollution, added traffic, property values, and effects on nearby wetlands and bird migration. Forest Grove Mayor Malynda Wenzl acknowledged residents' frustration over the buildings' height. Crane's site lists a set of data-center compliance certifications it says it builds and operates to, including PCI DSS, ISO 27001, FISMA, NIST 800-53, HITRUST, SSAE 18, and LEED, though as of this writing the Oregon campus remained under construction and had not yet opened to tenants.

reading.body:
Crane Data Centers is developing over 100 megawatts of capacity in the Portland metro area through a joint venture with Principal Asset Management, an institutional infrastructure investor, but the company has not published how much is currently operating versus still under construction.

The partnership structure mirrors a broader pattern in data center development where specialized operators pair with large capital providers to fund regional buildouts. Crane's emphasis on renewable energy access and site selection suggests the company is positioning around power availability, a critical constraint in the Pacific Northwest for any large AI infrastructure investment. The contested local approval process for the Forest Grove facility reflects the land use friction that large data center proposals now routinely encounter in growing metropolitan areas, even in regions with established tech industries like Oregon's Silicon Forest.

The data does not cover Crane's total company-wide capacity, headquarters location, or founding date, so the scale of this developer relative to national operators cannot be assessed from published sources. It also does not specify what portion of the announced 100+ megawatts is already serving customers or what timeline remains for the remainder of the campus build, which matters for understanding when this capacity will actually be available to consume power and support compute workloads.
